lesson.title: Cutting the Cord Without Losing the LAN
lesson.summary: A wireless LAN delivers the same local-network experience as a wired Ethernet LAN using radio waves as the medium, which forces extra data-link-layer machinery to cope with a shared, contested, half-duplex channel.
lesson.body:
Every local area network needs some physical way to move bits between devices, and for decades that meant copper or fiber Ethernet cable. A wireless LAN keeps the same basic goal, a group of nearby devices sharing one local network, but replaces the cable with radio waves traveling through open air. This single substitution changes almost everything about how the network behaves beneath the surface, even though from the perspective of an application or a user, a wireless LAN looks and acts like an ordinary LAN.

The wireless medium is fundamentally different from a cable. A cable is a private path that only the two connected devices use; radio waves spread outward and are received by anything with an antenna in range, including devices that are not part of the network, plus interference from microwaves, neighboring networks, and physical obstructions. A wired LAN built on switches gives every device an essentially private full duplex link to the switch. A wireless LAN, by contrast, is a shared, half duplex broadcast medium: only one nearby device can transmit at a time without colliding, and every station has to listen before speaking.

This has direct consequences at the data link layer. Wired Ethernet historically detected collisions by listening while transmitting, since a station's own weak received signal was easy to distinguish from what it was sending. A wireless radio transmitting at full power cannot reliably hear a much weaker colliding signal arriving at the same instant. So wireless LANs use collision avoidance rather than collision detection, listening before transmitting and using randomized backoff timers to reduce the chance that two stations start at the same moment.

Picture a small office with eight laptops and a wireless router. A wired LAN's switch would give those same eight laptops eight private cables, and any two of them could exchange data at full speed simultaneously without interference from the other six. On a wireless LAN, all eight laptops effectively share one channel, one piece of spectrum, so if two employees start a video call at the same moment, they are contending for the same limited airtime rather than each getting an independent private path, and the throughput each one experiences drops as more devices actively transmit.

This shared, contested nature of the wireless medium is exactly why wireless LANs need mechanisms that wired networks never required: careful channel planning, access points to organize who talks to whom, and coordination protocols to avoid collisions, all of which the concepts that follow build out in detail. A wireless LAN is still a LAN in every functional sense; it simply has to work much harder at the physical and data link layers to deliver that experience over a medium nobody can privately own.
